record.context_brief: Injectivity of the classical Radon transform
record.original_question: Let f be a continuous function on R^2 such that for every straight line l_{alpha,p} = {x in R^2 : alpha · x = p}, where alpha is a unit vector and p is real, the line integral of f over that line is zero: Rf := integral over l_{alpha,p} of f ds = 0. Assume also that f is integrable on every such line and satisfies the polynomial growth bound |f(x)| <= c(1 + |x|^m) for some constants c > 0 and m >= 0. Must it follow that f is identically zero? Equivalently, what is the weakest natural growth condition at infinity that still makes the classical Radon transform injective for such continuous functions?

evidence.quote: Assume that f ∈ L1(ℓα,p) for all p and α, that f is a continuous function, and that |f(x)| ≤ c(1 + |x|^m), where c = const > 0, and m ≥ 0 is a fixed number. Assume that Rf = 0 for all p and α. Problem 1: Does it follow from the above assumptions that f = 0?

The open problem is to understand what the weakest natural restriction on the growth of f at infinity is for the Radon transform to be injective. In other words, under what weakest growth restriction at infinity do assumptions (1) and (3) imply f = 0?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $f:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$ be a continuous function. For each unit vector $\alpha\in S^1$ and each $p\in\mathbb{R}$, let $\ell_{\alpha,p}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^2:\alpha\cdot x=p\}$ and assume that $f\in L^1(\ell_{\alpha,p})$ (with respect to arclength measure $ds$). Define the classical Radon transform of $f$ by
$$(Rf)(\alpha,p)=\int_{\ell_{\alpha,p}} f\,ds.$$
Assume in addition that there exist constants $c>0$ and $m\ge 0$ such that
$$|f(x)|\le c\,(1+|x|^m)\qquad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb{R}^2.$$
Suppose $(Rf)(\alpha,p)=0$ for every unit vector $\alpha$ and every $p\in\mathbb{R}$.

(a) Must $f\equiv 0$?

(b) More generally, determine the weakest natural growth restriction on $f$ at infinity, compatible with $f$ being continuous and integrable on every line, under which the vanishing of $Rf$ on all lines forces $f\equiv 0$.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of injectivity of the classical Radon transform for continuous functions with polynomial growth is listed as an open problem by Ramm. Classical injectivity results hold for rapidly decaying functions (e.g., Schwartz class) and counterexamples exist for slowly decaying functions, but the sharp/weakest natural growth condition that still guarantees injectivity (and in particular whether polynomial growth $|f(x)|\le c(1+|x|^m)$ together with line-integrability suffices) does not appear to have been settled in the literature found.

status_evidence.title: Three open problems in analysis (arXiv:math/0603631)
status_evidence.snippet: Problem 1 asks whether continuity, integrability on every line, polynomial growth and vanishing Radon transform imply f=0; the weakest growth condition for injectivity is stated as open.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is stated as open.

status_evidence.title: Some open problems in analysis, A.G. Ramm
status_evidence.snippet: Ramm lists the injectivity of the classical Radon transform under minimal growth assumptions among unresolved problems.
status_evidence.claim: Listed as an open problem by Ramm.
